analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare offer its own prescription drug plan that negotiates drug prices directly, alongside private plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in February 2013 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it died without a vote or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a government-run prescription drug plan that any Medicare beneficiary could choose, alongside the private plans that currently dominate Medicare Part D. Medicare would negotiate drug prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers for that plan, using buying power similar to other government programs like the VA. The goal was to lower drug costs for seniors, since private plans are barred by law from negotiating prices on behalf of the whole program. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, particularly seniors paying high out-of-pocket prescription drug costs, would gain a cheaper government-run plan option. Because Medicare would negotiate prices directly with drugmakers instead of relying on private insurers' rebates, the plan's premiums and cost-sharing could be lower than comparable private plans. The competitive pressure could also push private insurers to trim their own premiums.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer at least one government-run prescription drug plan available nationwide, alongside private plans.
It directs the Secretary to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce the purchase cost of covered drugs, using strategies similar to other federal purchasers such as the VA.

It builds a national formulary based on clinical benefit and price, designed to steer coverage toward drugs that cost less and work as well or better, and requires an appeals process for beneficiaries denied non-formulary drugs when medically necessary.
It sets a uniform national premium based on the actual cost of running the plan, rather than private insurers' marketing and profit margins.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face direct government negotiation over drug prices for the first time in Medicare Part D, and private drug plan insurers, who would face a new government-run competitor. Some industry revenue lost to lower negotiated prices could translate into reduced investment in new drug development.

drawbacks.text: The government-run plan would use a national formulary with tools like tiered copayments, prior authorization, and step therapy, which could limit some beneficiaries' access to specific drugs or require trying cheaper alternatives first.

A Medicare-operated plan competing with private insurers could draw enrollment away from private Part D plans, and opponents of this approach have argued it could eventually displace private coverage and reduce pharmaceutical companies' revenue for research on new medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit—direct government negotiation to lower drug prices for millions of seniors—would likely be substantial, and a competing public plan could also push private insurers to hold down premiums. The main drawbacks are design concerns: a government-run national formulary using tiered copays, prior authorization, and step therapy could restrict which drugs are covered, and opponents argued that government competition could eventually crowd out private plans and that negotiation power could suppress investment in new medicines. Those tradeoffs were never publicly tested because the bill never received a committee vote or floor debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The only action ever taken was referral to the Finance Committee on February 28, 2013; no hearings, markups, committee vote, or floor action followed.
The bill died in committee when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and private Medicare drug insurers, who kept the current Part D structure without government price negotiation or a competing public plan.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on February 28, 2013.

for.name: Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress—no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed letting Medicare negotiate drug prices or compete with private plans, a position widely reported across the era's Part D negotiation debates.

sides.party_line_note: Both cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Senate Democrat leader; no Republicans supported it, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee nonetheless never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would end their freedom from price negotiation in Medicare Part D, letting the government negotiate purchase prices directly. Industry lobbying was widely reported as a major reason Medicare negotiation proposals repeatedly stalled in Congress.
A nationwide government-run plan would compete with private Part D plans for enrollees, potentially shrinking their role in the program.
Lower reimbursement rates from a negotiated government plan could squeeze pharmacy margins, though broader drug affordability could increase adherence and volume.
